match.reason: No bank point teaches the split of government spending into current, capital and transfer payments; e-govtrade only defines government spending within aggregate demand and excludes transfers, and the other matches cover fiscal policy, budget outcomes or unrelated topics.

draft.title: Government spending
card: Current spending
spending on the day-to-day running of services, such as wages for public servants, teachers and nurses, and the cost of running hospitals and schools.
Capital spending
spending on long-lasting assets that are used for many years, such as roads, railways, hospitals and school buildings.
Transfer payments
money paid to people with no good or service given back in return, such as the Age Pension and JobSeeker Payment.
Transfer payments move income from one group to another. They are not payment for work, so the government does not receive output in exchange.
draft.remember: Current runs services now, capital builds assets that last, and transfers pass money to people.

a.q: Which of these is an example of government capital spending?
opts: Building a new railway line between two suburbs
Paying the wages of nurses in a public hospital
Paying the Age Pension to retired people
Buying paper and power for a public school
a.why: A railway line is a long-lasting asset used for many years, so it is capital spending. Nurses' wages are tempting, but they pay for a service delivered now, which is current spending.
a.clue: Which one is an asset that lasts for many years?

b.q: Last year the Victorian Government paid teachers' wages, built a new hospital wing and paid carer payments to families. Which row matches these in order?
opts: Current, capital, transfer
Capital, current, transfer
Current, transfer, capital
Transfer, capital, current
b.why: Teachers' wages pay for a service now, so they are current. A hospital wing lasts for years, so it is capital. Carer payments are given with nothing supplied in return, so they are transfers. Wages can look like transfers because money goes to people, but the government receives work in exchange.
b.clue: Ask of each item: is it a service now, a lasting asset, or money with nothing supplied back?

a.best: Building a new railway line between two suburbs

problems.detail: The question says the Victorian Government paid carer payments to families, but Carer Payment (like other income-support transfers) is paid by the Commonwealth through Services Australia. The chapter is about the Commonwealth budget, so the scenario should use the Australian Government, or an item a state actually pays.

check.summary: Question b wrongly has the Victorian Government paying carer payments, which are a Commonwealth transfer, in a chapter about the Commonwealth budget. The rest of the point is accurate, and both questions have one clear right answer.
